adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a regression. Looking at the diff for `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6`, the public group members route now calls `model.findMembers()` which uses the new pagination with `limit: 50`. However, examining `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs`, the template only iterates over `members` with no pagination controls (unlike the admin template which has next/previous buttons). The old code in `findMembers` returned all members directly, but now it's limited to 50 with no way for users to see more on the public group members page. This is a real functional regression where groups with >50 members will have inaccessible members on the public view.

Looking at the diff, the old code used `params[:group][:name]` and `params[:group][:usernames]` etc., while the new code uses `params[:name]`, `params[:visible]`, etc. directly. However, this is an intentional API change - the controller is being refactored to use flat parameters instead of nested ones. The corresponding JavaScript changes in the diff show `group.js` was also updated: the old `asJSON` returned `{ group: {...} }` but the new version returns just `{...}`. The frontend and backend changes are coordinated, so there's no compatibility issue within this PR. The finding incorrectly assumes existing clients would break, but the diff shows the client code is being updated simultaneously.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that PATCH requests with `changes: {add: username}` or `changes: {delete: username}` would now silently fail. However, looking at the diff, the old controller had separate `update_patch` and `update_put` methods dispatched based on request type. The new controller completely removes the PATCH-specific handling - there is no longer any code path that handles the `changes` parameter format. The old PATCH endpoint functionality (incremental add/delete via `changes` param) has been replaced with new dedicated endpoints: `add_members` (PUT /members) and `remove_member` (DELETE /members). The finding incorrectly assumes PATCH requests would still be routed to the update action and processed incorrectly, but the routes.rb changes show the API has been restructured entirely. Old PATCH clients would get a different response (likely 404 or method not allowed), not silent success with wrong behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js:31 — [confidence 100][P2] `self.setProperties({` unconditionally applies every asynchronous member response, so clicking Next twice while requests overlap lets the slower first response overwrite the newer page and offset with stale results because no request identity or in-flight guard rejects obsolete responses.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in the findMembers function. Looking at the diff, when findMembers() is called, it makes an async AJAX request and then unconditionally calls self.setProperties() with the response data including offset, limit, user_count, and members. If a user clicks 'next' twice quickly, two requests are fired. If the second request completes before the first, the first (stale) response will overwrite the correct data when it eventually completes. The code has no request cancellation, sequence tracking, or guard to reject obsolete responses. This is a real race condition bug in the pagination implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js:47 — [confidence 75][P2] `self.findMembers();` is neither returned nor given a rejection handler in both membership mutation callbacks, so a successful add or removal followed by a failed refresh resolves the mutation promise successfully and leaves administrators looking at stale membership with no refresh failure surfaced.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff in app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js, the `addMembers` and `removeMember` functions both call `self.findMembers()` in their `.then()` callbacks but don't return the result. The `findMembers()` method returns a promise (Discourse.ajax call). If `findMembers()` fails after a successful add/remove, the outer promise from `addMembers`/`removeMember` will still resolve successfully because the inner promise rejection is not propagated. This means the UI would show success even though the member list refresh failed, leaving stale data displayed. This is a real bug - the promise chain is broken.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `addMembers` at line 64 calls `this.get("model").addMembers(this.get("usernames"))` without handling the returned promise, and `removeMember` at line 56 calls `self.get("model").removeMember(member)` inside a bootbox callback also without error handling. Looking at the model code in the diff, both `addMembers` and `removeMember` return promises from `Discourse.ajax`. If these AJAX calls fail, there's no `.catch()` or error handler to notify the user, unlike the `save` action which has proper error handling with `disableSave` state management. This is a real defect where failed membership operations would silently fail without user feedback.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:71 — [confidence 75][P2] `usernames.split(",").each do |username|` invokes a String method on an untyped required parameter, so an authenticated request with `usernames[]=alice` passes parameter presence validation and raises NoMethodError instead of returning a validation response.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in the `add_members` action at line 71, `params.require(:usernames)` returns whatever type is passed. If a client sends `usernames[]=alice` (an array), Rails will return an array, and calling `.split(",")` on an array will raise NoMethodError. The code does not validate that `usernames` is a String before calling `.split()`. This is a real bug where malformed input causes an unhandled exception instead of a proper validation error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/admin/groups_controller_spec.rb:107 — [confidence 100, P2, advisory] The replacement membership specs (`group.users.count.should == 2` here and `group.users.count.should == 0` at line 129) accept destructive implementations that replace all members on addition or delete all members on removal because addition starts with an empty group and removal starts with only the target, leaving administrators of populated groups unprotected against loss of unrelated memberships; the strongest rebuttal is that both tests inspect real persisted associations, but neither supplies a surviving member and the diff deletes the prior incremental-add/non-member-removal coverage, so preservation must be asserted using existing members and exact remaining identities.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap in the new specs. Looking at the diff, the add_members test at line 107 starts with an empty group and adds 2 users, checking count==2. The remove_member test at line 129 starts with only 1 user and removes them, checking count==0. The finding is correct that these tests don't verify that existing unrelated members are preserved during add/remove operations. The diff also shows deletion of prior incremental tests that had some coverage for this. However, this is a test quality concern, not a bug in the actual implementation code. The implementation in groups_controller.rb uses group.add(user) and group.users.delete(user_id) which are standard Rails association methods that should preserve other members. This is a valid test coverage concern but not a defect.
